questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Habitat and Abiotic Factors' refers to.
questions.a: Every organism lives in a habitat that supplies food, shelter and mates, and the habitat is shaped by four major abiotic components: temperature, water, light and soil, together with the physico-chemical features of the substratum and atmosphere.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Habitat and Abiotic Factors'.
questions.a: Ecology at the organism level is basically the study of how an organism meets the stresses these abiotic factors impose.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Habitat and Abiotic Factors' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Organism and Its Environment (source: lebo111.txt unit introduction, habitat definition and abiotic factor sections)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Responses to Abiotic Stress' refers to.
questions.a: Organisms cope with unfavourable temperature and water conditions in four ways: regulate internal conditions (homeostasis like mammals and birds), simply conform to the ambient conditions, migrate temporarily to more suitable habitats, or suspend activity (diapause, hibernation, aestivation).

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Responses to Abiotic Stress'.
questions.a: Only a small fraction of animals are true regulators; most are conformers because thermoregulation is energetically expensive.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Responses to Abiotic Stress' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Responses to Abiotic Factors (source: lebo111.txt regulate-conform-migrate-suspend section and desert lizard example)

questions.q: Using the method 'Population Growth Models', work with: k_cap = 8, n_pop = 120, r_rate = 15. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of instantaneous_growth.
Take the relation taught for 'Population Growth Models' and work with: k_cap = 45, n_pop = 200, r_rate = 8. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of instantaneous_growth.
Explain in your own words what 'Population Growth Models' refers to.
questions.a: Population density changes through natality, mortality, immigration and emigration; under unlimited resources growth is exponential (dN/dt = rN) while under the carrying capacity K of real habitats growth is logistic (dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K), giving a sigmoid curve.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Population Growth Models'.
questions.a: The term (K-N)/K weights growth down as N approaches carrying capacity, so computing it tells how much room a population still has to grow.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Population Growth Models', in plain ASCII form.
Explain in your own words what 'Population Interactions' refers to.
questions.a: Populations of different species interact as mutualism (both benefit), competition (both harmed), predation and parasitism (one benefits, other harmed), commensalism (one benefits, other unaffected) and amensalism (one harmed, other unaffected).

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Population Interactions'.
questions.a: Competition is best defined as a minus-minus interaction and its outcome may be competitive exclusion or resource partitioning (like the five closely related species of warblers on a single tree).

questions.q: Under which section is 'Population Interactions' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Population Interactions (source: lebo111.txt interaction table and warbler resource-partitioning example)
